title: AI in Hiring Process
text:
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to review and write resumes raises concerns about how it affects creativity, critical thinking, and a reviewer’s ability to recognize a candidate’s true qualifications. Many job applicants now use AI tools to improve grammar, organize information, and tailor resumes to job descriptions. At the same time, employers and hiring managers are also using AI systems to screen and evaluate applications more quickly. While these technologies can make hiring more efficient, they also raise important ethical concerns. One concern is how the use of AI may affect an applicant’s creativity and critical thinking skills. When AI generates resume content, it may reduce the need for individuals to reflect on their own experiences and communicate them in their own voice. Another concern is whether hiring managers can accurately recognize a candidate’s true qualifications when resumes are heavily assisted by AI. If many applicants use similar AI tools, resumes may begin to look alike, making it harder to distinguish genuine skills and experiences. For example, some companies have already reported an increase in AI-generated resumes, making it harder to distinguish between candidates and evaluate authentic qualifications. Overall, the growing use of AI in resume writing and review raises questions about fairness, transparency, and trust in the hiring process. This leads to the central question of this case:
Is it fair to use AI to write resumes in the hiring process?

title: Who it is impacting
text:
Click on a stakeholder to learn more about their role and how AI in hiring affects them.




Job Applicants





Job applicants are individuals who submit resumes when applying for jobs. Some applicants use AI tools to help write or improve their resumes, while others do not.


Impact



Applicants with access to AI tools may gain an advantage, while those without access may be rejected more often, even if equally qualified.


Increased competition may pressure all applicants to use AI tools, even if they prefer not to.



Interests



Fair evaluation of qualifications


Equal opportunity in hiring


Transparency in hiring decisions



Other Relevant Information


Applicants may have different levels of access to technology and different levels of experience using AI tools.







Resume Reviewers





Resume reviewers are individuals responsible for reading and evaluating resumes during the hiring process.


Impact



They may rely too heavily on AI tools, potentially overlooking strong candidates who do not match AI-generated patterns.


Their role may change or become reduced as automation increases.



Interests



Efficient review of applications


Accurate identification of qualified candidates


Reduced workload



Other Relevant Information


Their decisions directly affect which candidates move forward in the hiring process.







Human Resources (HR)





HR professionals manage hiring processes and ensure that companies follow hiring policies and employment laws.


Impact



They must balance efficiency with fairness while ensuring AI tools do not introduce discrimination.


They may face challenges in regulating and monitoring AI use.



Interests



Fair and legal hiring practices


Efficient hiring processes


Reliable evaluation methods



Other Relevant Information


HR departments are responsible for balancing efficiency with ethical responsibility.







AI Companies





AI companies develop the tools used to generate and evaluate resumes.


Impact



They benefit financially from increased AI use but are responsible for ensuring fairness and accuracy.


Poorly designed systems could contribute to bias in hiring.



Interests



Innovation and product development


User trust


Responsible technology use



Other Relevant Information


The design of AI systems can influence hiring outcomes.







The Environment





The environment represents natural resources affected by the operation of AI technology and data centers.


Impact



Increased use of AI contributes to higher energy and water consumption, which may negatively impact the environment over time.



Interests



Sustainable technology development


Reduced resource consumption



Other Relevant Information


Environmental impact is a long-term concern as AI use continues to grow.

title: Ethical Issues
text:
Click on an option to explore its ethical analysis and impacts.





Option 1: Allow AI Use With Disclosure





Applicants are allowed to use AI tools as long as they clearly disclose how AI was used in their application materials.


Pros



Improves efficiency in resume screening


Encourages transparency in applications



Cons



May reduce originality and critical thinking


AI bias could affect screening outcomes


Could disadvantage applicants without AI access



Impact on Stakeholders



Applicants may feel pressure to use AI tools


HR must enforce disclosure rules


Reviewers may still struggle with trust in resumes



Ethical Frameworks


Utilitarianism: Increases efficiency and clarity, but may introduce inequality and bias depending on AI access and model quality.


Deontology: Supports honesty and fairness through disclosure requirements, but relies heavily on compliance.


Virtue Ethics: Encourages honesty and responsibility, though it may weaken personal effort and creativity.








Option 2: AI Allowed Only for Grammar and Translation





AI tools may only be used for grammar correction and language translation, not for generating content or rewriting experience descriptions.


Pros



Reduces overreliance on AI


Supports non-native English speakers


Maintains fairness while allowing accessibility support



Cons



Hard to monitor compliance


May slow down application review processes slightly



Impact on Stakeholders



Applicants retain basic AI support


HR gets clearer usage guidelines


AI companies may see reduced usage



Ethical Frameworks


Utilitarianism: Balances fairness and accessibility while preserving human authorship of ideas.


Deontology: Creates a clear rule for acceptable AI use and promotes fairness.


Virtue Ethics: Encourages responsibility, honesty, and self-development.








Option 3: No AI Use Allowed





All AI use is prohibited for both applicants and resume reviewers throughout the hiring process.


Pros



Encourages original thinking and authenticity


Ensures equal rules for all applicants



Cons



Increases workload for reviewers


Disadvantages non-native speakers


Removes useful accessibility tools



Impact on Stakeholders



Applicants must rely entirely on their own writing skills


HR and reviewers face higher workload



Ethical Frameworks


Utilitarianism: Preserves authenticity but may reduce overall efficiency and accessibility.


Deontology: Ensures equal treatment but removes potentially helpful tools.


Virtue Ethics: Strongly supports independence, effort, and authenticity.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text: As explored on the home page, the rise of AI in hiring raises serious ethical questions about fairness, trust, and transparency. This page takes a closer look at each of those concerns and what they mean for both job applicants and employers.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text: As explored on the home page, the rise of AI in hiring raises serious ethical questions about fairness, trust, and transparency. This page takes a closer look at each of those concerns and what they mean for both job applicants and employers.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text:
Fairness
Fairness is one of the most immediate concerns. Applicants who use AI tools to tailor their resumes may have a significant advantage over those who do not, whether due to lack of access, lack of awareness, or a personal choice not to use AI. This creates an uneven playing field before anyone even reaches an interview.
Some applicants use AI as a shortcut to adjust a base resume for each job posting. Others go further by adding keywords specifically chosen to pass automated screening systems. In both cases, the resume may no longer reflect the applicant’s genuine qualifications. Research shows this trend is growing, as seen in the AI in Resume Review study and this NYT report.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text:
Transparency
Transparency matters because employers often have no way of knowing how much of a resume was written by AI. A hiring manager reading a polished, well-structured resume may assume it reflects the applicant’s own communication skills, when in reality it was heavily rewritten by a language model.
Some companies have begun experimenting with AI-detection tools, but these are unreliable and raise their own fairness concerns, particularly for non-native English speakers whose writing may be flagged incorrectly. The ProQuest ethics article explores this tension in depth.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text:
Bias
AI tools are not neutral. They are trained on existing data, which means they can reproduce and amplify existing biases in hiring. Research has shown that name-based discrimination remains a problem, and AI screening systems have been found to perpetuate this — see the name discrimination study for specific findings.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text:
Accessibility
Not everyone has equal access to AI tools. Premium AI writing assistants often require paid subscriptions, meaning applicants from lower-income backgrounds may not have access to the same tools as other candidates. This could widen existing inequalities in the job market rather than reducing them.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text:
Creativity & Trust
When employers suspect resumes are AI-generated, it erodes trust in the hiring process overall. At the same time, there are concerns that AI-assisted writing reduces an applicant’s creative self-expression and ability to communicate in their own voice — a concern examined directly in the AI & creativity research.

title: Introduction to Ethical Issues
text:
Discussion Questions

Is the connection between culture and applicants’ stories seen in applications? How has it changed?
Should employers treat AI-assisted resumes differently from fully human-written resumes? Why or why not?
Does access to AI technology create an unfair advantage for some applicants?
How can companies verify that the skills listed on resumes are genuine?
Should there be limits on how much AI can be used in the hiring process?

title: Intro
text:
The use of AI to write resumes raises concerns about fairness in hiring. Applicants who use AI tools may have an advantage over those who do not. For example, some applicants use AI as a shortcut to adjust their base resume to the job they are applying to. Another way that some use AI to their advantage is by adding keywords that they know the AI will identify as qualified. Employers may also struggle to determine whether resumes accurately represent a candidate’s real skills and experiences.
In addition to fairness, this ethical issue also raises concerns about trust, bias, and transparency. Transparency is important because employers may not know how much of a resume was generated by AI. Bias can occur if AI tools favor certain writing styles or backgrounds. Accessibility is a concern because not all applicants have equal access to AI tools. Trust is affected when employers are unsure whether resumes reflect genuine skills.

title: Ethical Issues
section: Below we will evaluate each option based on ethical frameworks
text:
Below we will evaluate each option based on ethical frameworks

Option 1: Allow Use of AI as Long as It Is Stated Utilitarianism: This option may create benefits by increasing efficiency in the hiring process. Applicants can produce clearer resumes, and employers can review applications more quickly. However, it may also create harm if applicants rely too heavily on AI, leading to less originality and difficulty identifying genuine skills. If the AI used is not well-trained, it may also introduce bias in applications from applicants from different backgrounds. Overall, this option could produce positive outcomes if transparency is required, but it may still create inequality between applicants who have access to AI tools and those who do not. Deontology: From a rule-based perspective, requiring applicants to disclose AI use supports fairness and honesty. Transparency allows employers to make informed decisions and maintain trust in the hiring process. However, enforcing this rule may be difficult, and some applicants may not follow it. Virtue Ethics: This option encourages honesty and responsibility by asking applicants to admit when AI was used. However, it may reduce personal effort and creativity if individuals depend too heavily on AI tools.


Option 2: Allow Use of AI Only for Grammar and Translation Utilitarianism: This option balances efficiency and fairness. Applicants can use AI to improve clarity and accessibility, especially for non-native English speakers, while still maintaining responsibility for their own ideas and experiences. This approach may produce the greatest overall benefit by supporting communication without replacing critical thinking. Deontology: This option follows a clear rule about acceptable AI use. It promotes fairness by allowing limited assistance while preventing misuse of AI-generated content. Virtue Ethics: This option supports responsibility, honesty, and self-development. Applicants still need to reflect on their experiences and communicate their own achievements.


Option 3: Do Not Allow Use of AI
Utilitarianism: This option protects creativity and authenticity, but it may also create negative consequences. Resume reviewers may experience a heavier workload, and applicants who struggle with writing or language barriers may be disadvantaged.
Deontology: A strict ban on AI may promote fairness by treating all applicants equally. However, it may also limit access to helpful tools that support communication and accessibility.
Virtue Ethics: This option strongly supports independence, effort, and authenticity. It encourages individuals to rely on their own skills rather than automated assistance.

title: Deeper Dive
text:
Recent studies and reports suggest that the use of AI in hiring has significantly changed how employers evaluate candidates. Many hiring managers report that they are reviewing large numbers of resumes that look very similar due to the use of AI tools. This can make it difficult to identify candidates who truly have the skills required for the job.

76% of hiring managers report that finding genuinely skilled candidates has become more difficult in the era of AI-enhanced resumes.
72% of talent acquisition leaders say they do not fully trust the self-reported skills listed on resumes and would prefer to base hiring decisions on validated skills instead.
Some companies are returning to in-person interviews due to increased AI-assisted cheating.

Some companies have also noticed an increase in AI-assisted cheating during job interviews, including the use of AI tools to generate answers or simulate responses. As a result, major companies have begun returning to in-person interviews to better assess candidates’ real abilities and reduce fraud. Another interesting trend is that employers are shifting their focus from what candidates know to how they apply their knowledge. Skills such as problem-solving, communication, and adaptability are becoming more important than simply listing qualifications on a resume.
There is also a contradiction in the job market:

Many individuals report difficulty finding employment
However, 67% of employers say they are experiencing a talent shortage

This suggests that the issue may not be a lack of applicants, but rather challenges in identifying qualified candidates in an AI-driven hiring environment.
